title: H6 – Rewards I: what to pay for and performance-related pay
source: Zusammenfassung von Session 6 „Rewards and compensation part 1“ (Renard, 2008; PRP-Fälle Safelite, City, Vatikan)

blocks.text: The key question is not “how much” but “what for”: pay depends on internal consistency, external competitiveness and individual contributions (Renard, 2008). Differences based on individual characteristics are unwise or illegal.
Job analysis feeds internal consistency (job evaluation) and external competitiveness (market pricing); together they form the salary structure.
Individual contributions can be rewarded as pay for skills (education, experience, abilities) or pay for performance (achievements, objectives, extra mile).
PRP might work through culture, sorting (keep the good), motivation (expectancy theory) and focused effort (agency theory).

Evidence is mixed: Safelite and jockeys show success, but employees often doubt PRP (Marsden et al., 2009). Practical problems: measurement, appraisal bias, need for precision, contingency & contiguity, administration cost.
What to pay for (Renard, 2008)
children: Internal consistency: abilities, duties, education, experience, complexity, job level
External competitiveness: ability to pay, cost of living, industry, market, profitability, size, unions, supply & demand

children: Job analysis → internal consistency + external competitiveness → salary structure

Agency theory

blocks.text: PRP cases
children: Safelite: measurable individual output, unpaid rework, pay floor → success
City bonuses (Stiglitz): rewards for short-term, risk-blind results – “paid to gamble”; escrow instead of caps
Vatican: subjective criteria, cultural clash, intrinsic motivation – no financial rewards for clergy

blocks.text: Explain each pay difference with Renard's three groups and the case facts.
For a PRP scheme, test expectancy theory link by link and the five practical problems.
Decide whether PRP fits: does the measure match the goal, does the employee control it, are results known before payment, who bears the cost of failure, does it fit motivation and culture?
Recommend design: quantity and quality measured, horizon matched to results, floor protected – and remember that PRP is only as good as the PM system behind it.
Pay reflects the relative value of jobs within the organisation.
Pay reflects what the relevant labour market pays.
Pay that varies with individual, team or organisational performance.
Belief that effort leads to performance; that performance leads to the reward; the value attached to the reward (Vroom).
The reward clearly depends on the performance / the reward follows the performance closely in time.
Can you build an argument regarding when and how performance-related pay might work? Use Safelite, the City and the Vatican as test cases.
The candle problem: why can incentives worsen performance on creative tasks?
